Version

2026-11

Agentic describes systems where LLMs plan, use tools and coordinate over many
steps with some autonomy. It covers a spectrum — from fixed workflows with LLM steps
to fully autonomous agents and multi-agent teams.

More autonomy = more flexibility, but also more cost, latency and risk.

These building blocks (popularised by Anthropic’s Building effective agents) cover most
real-world needs. Combine them.

Split a task into sequential steps; add checks (“gates”) between them.

Example: generate a SQL query → validate it with EXPLAIN → run → summarise.
Classify the input, then send it to a specialised prompt, tool or model.

Sectioning: split independent subtasks and run them at the same time.

Voting: run the same task several times and aggregate (more confidence).
A lead LLM breaks the task down dynamically, delegates to workers, then synthesises.
One LLM produces, another critiques against criteria, loop until good enough.

The model controls the loop itself (see agents). Use when the number of steps is
unpredictable and you trust the environment’s feedback (tests, query results…).

Architecture

How it works

Good for

Supervisor

One manager agent routes work to specialist sub-agents and merges results.

Most use cases; easy to debug.

Hierarchical

Supervisors of supervisors.

Large tasks (research, big codebases).

Handoffs / swarm

Agents pass control to each other directly.

Customer-support style flows.

Agent-as-a-tool

A sub-agent is exposed as a tool to a main agent; its context stays isolated.

Keeping the main context clean.

Multi-agent systems multiply tokens (often several times a single agent). Use them
when the task is truly parallel or needs isolated contexts — not by default.

Classic RAG retrieves once. Agentic RAG lets the agent decide if, where and how
many times to search: rewrite the query, choose between a vector index, SQL and web search,
check whether the evidence is sufficient, and search again if not.

🛡️ Guardrails

Least-privilege tools, read-only by default

Human approval for writes / payments / emails

Input & output validation, PII masking

Treat tool & web content as untrusted (prompt injection)

🔭 Observability

Trace every LLM call and tool call

OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, MLflow, Langfuse…

Log cost, latency, tokens per run

🧪 Evaluation

Final outcome: was the task solved?

Trajectory: right tools, right order, no loops?

Regression suite on every prompt/model change

💸 Cost & reliability

Step / token / time budgets

Retries with backoff, timeouts, idempotent tools

Cache prompts; cheap models for easy steps

Start simple — single call → workflow → agent → multi-agent, only when needed.

Make the plan visible — let the agent write its plan/to-do list.

Invest in tools — the agent-computer interface matters as much as the prompt.

Keep humans in the loop where errors are expensive.

Measure — no evals, no production.

Version

2026-11

An AI agent is an LLM that runs in a loop, decides which tools to call,
observes the results, and keeps going until the goal is reached.

Agent = Model + Instructions + Tools + Memory + Loop

Who decides the next step?

Example

Chatbot

Nobody — one question, one answer.

“Summarise this email.”

Workflow

Your code (fixed path, LLM inside some steps).

Extract invoice → validate → write to DB.

Agent

The model (dynamic path).

“Find why yesterday’s revenue dropped and draft a report.”

Start with the simplest thing that works. Most business problems are solved by a
single call or a workflow. Use an agent when the steps can’t be known in advance
and mistakes can be caught (tests, review, rollback).
This is often called ReAct (Reason + Act): think → act → observe → repeat.

1. Tools (function calling)

You describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema. The model answers
with a tool call (name + arguments); your code executes it and sends the result back.
Good tool descriptions matter as much as good prompts.

2. Memory

Short-term: the conversation and tool results in the context window.

Long-term: facts saved outside the model (files, database, vector store) and
retrieved later.

Long sessions need context management: summarise/compact or clear old tool results.

3. Planning

Breaking the goal into steps, sometimes written as an explicit to-do list the agent updates.

4. Environment & permissions

What the agent can touch (sandbox, files, APIs) and which actions need human approval.

Example with the Anthropic SDK (pip install anthropic). Every provider follows the
same pattern: send tools → model requests a call → you execute → send the result back.

import json
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic() # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

tools = [{
 "name": "get_revenue",
 "description": "Return total revenue in EUR for a given day (YYYY-MM-DD).",
 "input_schema": {
 "type": "object",
 "properties": {"day": {"type": "string"}},
 "required": ["day"],
 },
}]

def get_revenue(day: str) -> dict:
 return {"day": day, "revenue_eur": 125_400} # call your warehouse here

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Compare revenue of 2026-11-07 and 2026-11-08."}]

 })
 messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

print(next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

SDKs also ship helpers that run this loop for you (e.g. Anthropic’s tool runner), and
agent SDKs/frameworks (below) add built-in tools, memory and tracing.

MCP — Model Context Protocol

A2A — Agent2Agent protocol

Purpose

Connect an agent to tools and data (agent ↔ tool).

Let agents talk to other agents (agent ↔ agent).

Origin

Anthropic (Nov 2024), now an open standard under the Linux Foundation’s
Agentic AI Foundation.

Google (Apr 2025), now a Linux Foundation project.

Concepts

Host (app) → client → server exposing tools, resources, prompts.
Transports: stdio (local) or streamable HTTP (remote).

Agent card (capabilities), tasks, messages, artifacts.

Analogy

“USB-C for AI tools”

“HTTP between agents”

Write one MCP server for your API and every MCP-compatible client (Claude, ChatGPT,
IDEs, Snowflake/Databricks agents…) can use it.

Framework

Sweet spot

LangGraph

Stateful graphs with explicit control flow, checkpoints, human-in-the-loop.

CrewAI

Role-based multi-agent “crews”; quick to prototype.

LlamaIndex

Data/RAG-heavy agents, document workflows.

Pydantic AI

Type-safe Python agents with validated outputs.

Claude Agent SDK

The Claude Code harness as a library: file, shell and web tools, subagents, MCP.

OpenAI Agents SDK

Lightweight agents with handoffs and guardrails.

Google ADK

Agent Development Kit, integrates with Vertex AI and A2A.

Successor of AutoGen + Semantic Kernel for .NET / Python.

smolagents (Hugging Face)

Minimal “code agents” that write Python to act.

Inside data platforms: Snowflake Cortex Agents (see /data/snowflake) and
Databricks Agent Bricks (see /data/databricks) let you build agents next to your
governed data.

Few, well-named tools beat many overlapping ones.

Write descriptions as if for a new colleague: what it does, when to use it, input format.

Return concise, meaningful output (not 10 MB of JSON). Paginate.

Return clear errors the model can recover from (“unknown column revnue — did you mean revenue?”).

Make dangerous tools require confirmation; prefer read-only by default.

Version

2026-11

Generative AI models learn the patterns of huge datasets and generate new content
(text, code, images, audio…) one piece at a time. Large Language Models (LLMs) do it
for text by predicting the next token over and over.

Concept

What you need to know

Token

The unit an LLM reads and writes (≈ ¾ of an English word). Pricing, limits and speed
are all counted in tokens.

Context window

Max tokens the model can “see” at once (prompt + history + documents + answer).
Modern frontier models reach hundreds of thousands to ~1M tokens.

Transformer

The neural architecture behind LLMs. Attention lets every token look at every
other token in the context.

Pre-training

Learning to predict the next token on trillions of tokens of public text and code.

Post-training

Instruction tuning + preference training (RLHF / RLAIF) turns a raw model into a
helpful, safe assistant.

Reasoning models

Models that “think” (generate hidden reasoning) before answering. More thinking
(test-time compute) usually means better answers on hard tasks, at higher cost
and latency — often controlled by an effort setting.

Embeddings

inking
(test-time compute) usually means better answers on hard tasks, at higher cost
and latency — often controlled by an effort setting.

Embeddings

Vectors that represent the meaning of text. Similar meaning → close vectors.
The basis of semantic search and RAG.

Multimodal

Models that take images, PDFs, audio (and sometimes produce them) in addition to text.

Proprietary (API)

Anthropic — Claude (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku families)

OpenAI — GPT and o-series reasoning models

Google — Gemini

Usually the strongest models; you pay per token; data stays with the provider
(check retention terms).

Open-weight

Meta Llama, Mistral, Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek, Google Gemma…

Download the weights and self-host (vLLM, Ollama, TGI) or use a hosted endpoint
(Groq, Together, Databricks, Snowflake Cortex…).

Full control, fine-tunable, but you operate the infrastructure.

Pick the smallest model that passes your evaluation, not the biggest one.
Model names change every few months — your eval set is what lets you switch quickly.

Technique

When / how

System prompt

Define role, tone, rules and output format once, at the top.

Zero-shot

Just ask clearly. Works for most simple tasks with modern models.

Few-shot

Give 2–5 input → output examples to fix style or format.

Chain of thought

Ask the model to reason step by step (or use a reasoning model).

Structured output

Ask for JSON that follows a schema — most APIs can enforce a JSON schema.

Prompt chaining

Split a complex task into several smaller prompts (see agentic).

Delimiters

Wrap documents in tags (<document>…</document>) so the model knows what is data
and what is instruction.

A solid prompt skeleton

Wrap documents in tags (<document>…</document>) so the model knows what is data
and what is instruction.

A solid prompt skeleton

ROLE You are a senior data engineer reviewing SQL for a bank.
CONTEXT <schema> ... </schema>
TASK Review the query below for correctness and performance.
RULES - Only use tables from the schema. - Say "unknown" if unsure.
FORMAT JSON: {"issues": [{"line": int, "severity": "low|med|high", "fix": str}]}
INPUT <query> ... </query>

Climb only as high as you need — each step costs more.

Approach

Use it when…

Watch out for…

Prompting

Always the first step. Cheap and instant to iterate.

Long prompts cost tokens (use prompt caching).

RAG

The model needs your knowledge (docs, tickets, tables) or fresh data.

Retrieval quality is the bottleneck. See rag.

Tool use / agents

The model must act or fetch live data (APIs, SQL, search).

Loops, cost and safety. See agents.

Fine-tuning (LoRA / PEFT)

You need a specific style/format/behaviour at scale, or a smaller, cheaper model.

Needs quality labelled data; doesn’t add reliable knowledge.

Pre-training

Almost never. Only for labs or very specific domains.

Millions of dollars.

“It looks good on 3 examples” is not an evaluation.

Build a golden dataset — 50–200 real inputs with expected outputs or grading criteria.

Choose graders — exact match / code checks when possible; LLM-as-a-judge with a
clear rubric otherwise; humans for spot checks.

Track metrics — accuracy, faithfulness (no hallucination), relevance, latency, cost.

Run on every change (prompt, model, retrieval) like unit tests.

Useful tools: RAGAS, DeepEval, promptfoo, MLflow (GenAI evaluation & tracing),
Langfuse, Arize Phoenix.

Risk

Mitigation

Hallucination

Ground answers in retrieved sources, require citations, let the model say “I don’t know”.

Prompt injection

Treat retrieved/web/tool content as data, never instructions; least-privilege tools;
human approval for sensitive actions.

Data leakage / privacy

Mask PII, check provider data-retention, keep secrets out of prompts.

Cost & latency

Smaller models for easy steps, prompt caching, batching, streaming.

Bias & compliance

Evaluate on diverse cases; follow your regulation (e.g. the EU AI Act).

Temperature

Randomness of sampling. Low = deterministic, high = creative. Some recent reasoning
models fix it and expose an effort setting instead.

Hallucination

A fluent but false answer.

Grounding

Forcing the answer to rely on provided sources.

Prompt caching

Re-using an already-processed prompt prefix to cut cost and latency.

Guardrails

Input/output checks around a model (filters, validators, policies).

Quantization

Storing weights in fewer bits (8, 4…) to run models on smaller hardware.

RAG is one of the easiest ways to build LLM applications over your own data, however building a production-level RAG can be challenging. Here are five ways to improve your RAG pipeline:

Enhancing Retrieval : The retrieval aspect of RAG essentially functions as a search engine. Implementing hybrid retrieval techniques, combining lexical and vector-based methods, alongside cross-encoder re-ranking, can significantly enhance the retrieval of relevant data.

Data Standardization : Data utilized by RAG often originates from diverse sources, leading to varied formats and potential artifacts. Establishing a robust data preprocessing pipeline, whether through manual curation or leveraging LLM-based judgment, ensures proper standardization, filtering, and extraction of data, mitigating artifacts that may hinder the understanding by the LLM.

Crafting Effective Prompts : Effective application of RAG hinges not only on retrieving accurate context but also on prompt engineering. Crafting prompts that encompass relevant context and are formatted to elicit grounded responses from the LLM is crucial. Utilizing LLMs with expansive context windows and adopting strategies such as diversity and lost-in-the-middle selection facilitate optimal incorporation of context into prompts.

Rigorous Evaluation : Developing repeatable and accurate evaluation pipelines for RAG, assessing both the overall system performance and individual components, is imperative. Utilizing standard search metrics like DCG and nDCG for evaluating the retrieval pipeline and employing LLM-based judgment for evaluating the generation component ensures comprehensive assessment. Leveraging systems like RAGAS facilitates the evaluation of the complete RAG pipeline.

Continuous Data Collection : Post-deployment of the RAG application, ongoing data collection is vital for continual improvement. Strategies such as finetuning retrieval models based on relevant query-text pairs, refining LLMs using high-quality outputs, and conducting AB tests to quantitatively measure pipeline enhancements contribute to performance optimization over time.

The term Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was first introduced in a paper by a team at Facebook AI Research in 2020, as a way to improve the accuracy and reliability of generative AI models by fetching facts from external sources.

Initially, RAG focused on using unstructured data, but it has expanded to incorporate high-quality structured data, like knowledge graphs, to address issues like hallucinations and incorrect knowledge.

Recently, researchers have also started exploring self-retrieval, which involves using LLMs’ own knowledge to enhance their performance.

The image is from the paper ‘Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey’, last revised on Mar 2024; which should be a great read.

RAG combines the vast knowledge of LLMs with your data, enhancing AI’s ability to provide contextually rich responses.

It leverages existing LLM data and enriches it with your unique datasets through a process of loading, indexing, storing, querying, and evaluation.

Version

2026-11

Databricks is a lakehouse platform built by the creators of Apache Spark: your data
lives in open formats (Delta Lake / Iceberg) in your cloud storage, Unity Catalog
governs it, and you run SQL, Python, ML and AI agents on top.

Lakehouse = the cheap, open storage of a data lake + the reliability and performance
of a data warehouse. The bronze/silver/gold layering is the medallion architecture.

Component

enforcement. UniForm exposes Delta tables as Iceberg too.

metrics, and governance of models/functions/agents. Open-sourced.

Compute

SQL warehouses (Photon engine).

Jobs (orchestration, formerly Workflows), Designer (no-code).

# Read raw JSON, clean it, write a Delta table governed by Unity Catalog
raw = spark.read.json("/Volumes/main/landing/orders/")
clean = (raw.dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
 .filter("amount > 0"))
clean.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("main.silver.orders")

SQL (MERGE / time travel)

MERGE INTO main.silver.customers AS t
USING updates AS s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

-- Time travel
SELECT * FROM main.silver.customers VERSION AS OF 12;

Version

Snowflake is a fully managed cloud data platform (AWS, Azure, GCP) where storage and
compute are separated, you mostly speak SQL, and — since 2024–2026 — you can run
AI functions and agents directly on your governed data.

Layer

Role

Storage

Data stored once in compressed, columnar micro-partitions (or open Apache Iceberg
tables in your own bucket).

Compute

Virtual warehouses (XS → 6XL) that you start, stop, resize independently. Many
warehouses can read the same data without contention. Billed per second in credits.

Cloud services

Authentication, metadata, query optimisation, transactions, security & governance.

Feature

What it gives you

Time Travel & Fail-safe

Zero-copy cloning

Instant copy of a table/schema/database for dev or tests — no extra storage until changes.

Snowpipe / Snowpipe Streaming

Continuous, near-real-time ingestion from files or streams.

Openflow

Managed ingestion/integration service (based on Apache NiFi) with many connectors.

-- Compute: a warehouse that sleeps after 60 s of inactivity
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS transform_wh
 WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;

-- Time Travel: data as it was 5 minutes ago
SELECT * FROM orders AT (OFFSET => -60 * 5);

-- Zero-copy clone for a dev environment
CREATE DATABASE analytics_dev CLONE analytics;

-- Declarative pipeline kept fresh within 15 minutes
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE daily_sales
 TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes'
 WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
AS
 SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue
 FROM orders
 GROUP BY order_date;

-- Classify and filter reviews with LLMs, in plain SQL
SELECT
 review_id,
 AI_CLASSIFY(review_text, ['delivery', 'product', 'price', 'support']):labels[0] AS topic,
 AI_SENTIMENT(review_text) AS sentiment
FROM reviews
WHERE AI_FILTER(PROMPT('Is this customer asking for a refund? {0}', review_text));

SELECT AI_COMPLETE('llama3.1-70b', 'Summarise in one line: ' || ticket_body)
FROM support_tickets LIMIT 10;

That is a new way of handling either your environment variables or your configuration files.

Python Decouple helps you to separate settings from code. It allows you to define your settings in environment variables .env or µ.ini files,
and then access them in your Python code.

Example of .env file:

DEBUG=True
TEMPLATE_DEBUG=True
SECRET_KEY=ARANDOMSECRETKEY
DATABASE_URL=mysql://myuser:mypassword@myhost/mydatabase
PERCENTILE=90%
#COMMENTED=42 <- this is a commented line

Example of a settings.ini file:

[settings]
DEBUG=True
TEMPLATE_DEBUG=%(DEBUG)s
SECRET_KEY=ARANDOMSECRETKEY
DATABASE_URL=mysql://myuser:mypassword@myhost/mydatabase
PERCENTILE=90%%
#COMMENTED=42 <- this is a commented line

To use Python Decouple, you need to install it first. You can do this using pip:

mydatabase
PERCENTILE=90%%
#COMMENTED=42 <- this is a commented line

To use Python Decouple, you need to install it first. You can do this using pip:

pip install python-decouple

Then, you can use it in your Python code like this:

from decouple import config, Csv

DEBUG = config('DEBUG', default=False, cast=bool)
TEMPLATE_DEBUG = config('TEMPLATE_DEBUG', default=DEBUG, cast=bool)
SECRET_KEY = config('SECRET_KEY')
DATABASE_URL = config('DATABASE_URL')
PERCENTILE = config('PERCENTILE', default=90, cast=int)
ALLOWED_HOSTS = config('ALLOWED_HOSTS', default='localhost', cast=Csv())
TIMEOUT = config('TIMEOUT', default=5.0, cast=float)

It allows you to specify the type of the variable you want to retrieve.

Example of usage of the cast parameter:

>>> os.environ['DEBUG'] = 'False'
>>> config('DEBUG', cast=bool)
False

>>> os.environ['EMAIL_PORT'] = '42'
>>> config('EMAIL_PORT', cast=int)
42

>>> os.environ['ALLOWED_HOSTS'] = '.localhost, .herokuapp.com'
>>> config('ALLOWED_HOSTS', cast=lambda v: [s.strip() for s in v.split(',')])
['.localhost', '.herokuapp.com']

>>> os.environ['SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER'] = 'HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO, https'
>>> config('SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER', cast=Csv(post_process=tuple))
('HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO', 'https')

>>> os.environ['LIST_OF_INTEGERS'] = '1,2,3,4,5'
>>> config('LIST_OF_INTEGERS', cast=Csv(int))
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

))
('HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO', 'https')

>>> os.environ['LIST_OF_INTEGERS'] = '1,2,3,4,5'
>>> config('LIST_OF_INTEGERS', cast=Csv(int))
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

>>> os.environ['COMPLEX_STRING'] = '%virtual_env%\t *important stuff*\t trailing spaces '
>>> csv = Csv(cast=lambda s: s.upper(), delimiter='\t', strip=' %*')
>>> csv(os.environ['COMPLEX_STRING'])
['VIRTUAL_ENV', 'IMPORTANT STUFF', 'TRAILING SPACES']

Allows for cast and validation based on a list of choices. For example:

>>> from decouple import config, Choices
 >>> os.environ['CONNECTION_TYPE'] = 'usb'
 >>> config('CONNECTION_TYPE', cast=Choices(['eth', 'usb', 'bluetooth']))
 'usb'

 >>> os.environ['CONNECTION_TYPE'] = 'serial'
 >>> config('CONNECTION_TYPE', cast=Choices(['eth', 'usb', 'bluetooth']))
 Traceback (most recent call last):
 ...
 ValueError: Value not in list: 'serial'; valid values are ['eth', 'usb', 'bluetooth']

 >>> os.environ['SOME_NUMBER'] = '42'
 >>> config('SOME_NUMBER', cast=Choices([7, 14, 42], cast=int))
 42

Why use Python Decouple and not just os.environ ?

os.environ <— returns strings only, so you have to convert them to the right type manually.

Python Decouple <— allows you to specify the type of the variable directly in the config function using the cast parameter.

Everyone knows: Python is slow — especially when it comes to loops.

Instead of vectorizing everything or rewriting your logic in C/C++, there’s a hidden gem that deserves more attention: Numba.

Numba is a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler for Python, powered by LLVM. It takes your regular Python functions and compiles them into native machine code.

Result? Performance close to C, without leaving Python.

The apply method in Pandas is typically something we try to avoid,
as it often slows down code execution significantly.

But sometimes, we simply have no other choice.

So, how can we speed up apply without installing any extra libraries?

Since version 2.2, it’s possible to run the function using Numba instead of plain Python, thanks to the engine parameter.

Numba enables faster computation by compiling the code using the Just-In-Time (JIT) method to optimize performance.

Moreover, operations can now be parallelized, further boosting execution speed.

This tutorial is designed for data scientists who usually run scripts with:

python script.py

We will show you how to transform such scripts into a real Command-Line Interface (CLI).
First, we start with a very simple library called click.
Then, we move on to a modern, professional stack with Typer, Rich, Questionary, and Pyfiglet.

source:

Execute the script with:

uv run src/tuto_cli/cli_basic.py total 10 3 --taxes 20

Output:

💰 Price: 10.0 € x 3 = 30.00 €
➕ Taxes: 20.0% → Total = 36.00 €

Minimal features: no colors, no tables, no progress bars.

No interactivity: you cannot ask the user for confirmation or choices.

Low maintenance: cli is not widely used or updated.

Poor documentation compared to modern frameworks.

This is why we now move on to a modern stack.

Add the following libraries:

uv add typer[all] rich questionary pyfiglet

Open src/tuto_cli/cli.py :

import typer
import pyfiglet
import questionary
from rich.console import Console

app = typer.Typer()
console = Console()

@app.command()
def total(
 price: float = typer.Option(..., "--price", "-p", help="Unit price in euros"),
 quantity: int = typer.Option(..., "--quantity", "-q", help="Number of items"),
 taxes: float = typer.Option(0.0, "--taxes", "-t", help="Tax rate (%)"),
):
 """
 Compute the total cost of items, optionally with taxes.
 """

 # Pyfiglet banner
 banner = pyfiglet.figlet_format("Total CLI")
 console.print(f"[bold cyan]{banner}[/bold cyan]")

 # Confirmation with Questionary
 confirm = questionary.confirm(
 f"Do you want to calculate {quantity} item(s) at {price}€ with {taxes}% taxes?"
 ).ask()

Typer + Rich + Questionary + Pyfiglet turns your script into a professional tool.

For data scientists, this means you can share cleaner, friendlier tools with colleagues, automate pipelines, and create impressive demos.

text:
uv is a modern Python package manager that simplifies the management of Python environments and dependencies. It is designed to be user-friendly and efficient, making it easier for developers to work with Python projects.

Installation of uv (if not already installed)

Linux

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Powershell

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Start a new project with uv

uv init --package keyrus_tuto_uv

A note that the uv init command creates a new directory named keyrus_tuto_uv and initializes a new uv project in it. You can replace keyrus_tuto_uv with any name you prefer for your project.

Adding the –package option will allow you to directly create a Python package

Navigate to the project directory

cd keyrus_tuto_uv

[tool.commitizen]

]

fast-stack-forge is a powerful, Symfony-style CLI scaffolder designed to bootstrap and accelerate the development of FastAPI and Data Science applications. It provides a robust, production-ready directory structure, fully integrated with uv for lightning-fast package management, alongside essential utilities like rate limiting, scheduling, WebSocket management, dbt pipelines, and JWT middleware.

Rapid Scaffolding: Generate full FastAPI projects or AstroData-style Data Science repositories in seconds.

Entity Generation: Automatically create database models, Pydantic schemas, business logic controllers, and router endpoints for your entities.

Data Science Skeletons: Bootstrap data science structures, environment setups, Pytest suites, and interactive Streamlit pages.

AI Service Integration: Instantly scaffold Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), tool-calling Agents, stateful Agentic workflows (LangGraph), and OCR/Vision extraction services.

dbt (Data Build Tool) Support: Built-in commands to initialize and manage analytical engineering pipelines.

Data Synchronization: Scaffolds ELT/sync scripts to move data from NoSQL (e.g., MongoDB) to relational systems (e.g., PostgreSQL) with background scheduling.

nchronization: Scaffolds ELT/sync scripts to move data from NoSQL (e.g., MongoDB) to relational systems (e.g., PostgreSQL) with background scheduling.

Production-Ready Utilities: Pre-configured JWT middleware, rate limiting (slowapi), background tasks (apscheduler), and WebSockets.

Since fast-stack-forge leverages uv for lightning-fast environment and dependency setup, the recommended approach is to install it globally using the uv tool:

uv tool install fast-stack-forge

Alternatively, you can install it using standard pip:

pip install fast-stack-forge

To bootstrap a new FastAPI project, run the init command. You can specify your preferred database engine:

fast-stack-forge init my_project --db sqlite

Supported Database Engines (via --db option):

sqlite (default)

postgresql

mysql

mongodb

Navigate into your newly created project and install dependencies using uv:

cd my_project
make install
source .venv/bin/activate

Start the development server:

make run
FastForge integrates closely with AstroData to scaffold data science project structures.

Scaffold a complete data science structure with interactive questions:

fast-stack-forge init:ds-data my_ds_project --api --data

Options:

--api: Include a FastAPI REST API skeleton in src/<package_name>/api/.

--data: Include raw, interim, processed, and external ETL folders under data/.

Interactive Prompts:
When run, the command will prompt for:
1. Companion FastAPI project? (Asks to create a separate <name>_api project alongside).
2. Python version (Interactive selector list based on your system python).
3. Open-source license (MIT, BSD-3-Clause, Apache-2.0, GPL-3.0, or Proprietary).
4. Project description, Author Name, and Author Email.

section: Adding Backend Capabilities to Existing Projects (init:ds-make)
text:
If you already have a data science project, you can inject a FastAPI + Streamlit backend & dashboard into it:

cd my_ds_project
fast-stack-forge init:ds-make

This automatically detects the package structure inside src/ and creates:

src/<package>/api/ — FastAPI application structure and router.

app/<package>_app.py — Streamlit dashboard pre-wired to the API.

.streamlit/config.toml — Streamlit styles & port settings.

docker-compose.yml and dockerfiles/ — Preconfigured containerization.
FastForge provides standard Symfony-style maker commands for database entities.

Generate the database model, schema (Pydantic), controller, and API routes automatically:

fast-stack-forge make:entity Product name:string price:float category:string:fk=Category is_available:bool description:text:nullable

Field Syntax Definition:

Fields are defined as name:type[:modifier].

Supported Types: string, int, float, bool, text, date, datetime

Supported Modifiers:
- nullable: Allows the database column/field to be null.
- encrypt: Automatically encrypts the field before writing to the database.
- hash: Hashes the field value (useful for passwords).
- fk=ModelName: Establishes a foreign key relationship with another entity.

Options:

--no-router: Skip generating API routes/router.

--no-controller: Skip generating business logic controller.

If you want to remove all files generated for an entity (model, schema, controller, router), run:

fast-stack-forge make:discard Product
FastForge includes native scaffolding for analytical engineering via dbt (Data Build Tool).

To set up a dbt project within your src/ folder:

fast-stack-forge init:etl my_dbt_project --archi medallion --connector local

Options:

``–archi`` (Architecture style):
- default (creates stg, int, mart layers)
- medallion (creates bronze, silver, gold layers)
- star (creates raw, dim, fact tables)

``–connector`` (Data Warehouse connector):
- local (DuckDB)
- snowflake
- bigquery
- postgres

To generate a new dbt model and its schema definition file:

fast-stack-forge make:dbt customer_orders --layer silver

Options:

--view: Materialize model as a SQL view.

--incremental: Generate incremental update block.

--python: Generate a Python model instead of standard SQL.

--layer <layer>: Choose a specific layer to place the model in (e.g. bronze, staging, mart).

Instantly generate fully-coded AI services and their API routers:

fast-stack-forge make:service rag_helper --type rag --provider openai --vector chroma

Options:

``–type``:
- rag: Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
- agent: Tool-calling agent.
- agentic: Stateful LangGraph workflow.
- ocr: Document parsing/Vision service.

``–provider``: openai, anthropic, mistral, gemini, or azure

``–vector``: chroma, qdrant, supabase, or upstash (RAG type only)

Generate scripts to replicate/sync data between database systems (NoSQL to Relational) powered by APScheduler for automated run intervals:

fast-stack-forge make:sync MongoToPg --source mongodb --dest postgres

Scaffold a multi-page Streamlit dashboard inside app/dashboard/ and register a make dashboard target in the project Makefile:

fast-stack-forge make:dashboard Atelier Analytics Chatbot

A standard project generated with fast-stack-forge init my_project produces the following structure:

my_project/
├── app/
│ ├── main.py ← FastAPI entrypoint
│ └── dashboard/ ← Streamlit pages (created via make:dashboard)
├── src/
│ └── my_project/
│ ├── entity/ ← Database models
│ ├── schema/ ← Pydantic schemas
│ ├── controller/ ← Business logic
│ ├── router/ ← API routes
│ ├── service/ ← AI services (created via make:service)
│ ├── data/ ← DB connection setup
│ ├── middleware/ ← JWTBearer authorization
│ └── utils/
│ ├── limiter.py ← slowapi rate limiting
│ ├── scheduling.py← apscheduler background tasks
│ ├── crud_router.py← Generic CRUD routing factory
│ └── connection_manager.py ← WS connection manager
├── Makefile
├── pyproject.toml
└── .env

When starting a new project (whether it is an AI application, mobile app, web app, or data engineering pipeline), cost shouldn’t be a barrier. Below is a curated list of free and limited tiers that allow you to build, deploy, and showcase your projects for free.

Building a RAG app requires an LLM provider, a Vector Database, and an orchestration framework.

Groq Cloud: Offers free API access to state-of-the-art models like Llama 3, Gemma, and Mixtral with high rate limits. Perfect for local prototyping.

Pinecone: Provides a free starter index with up to 2GB storage, which is more than enough for thousands of document embeddings.

Qdrant Cloud: Offers a free tier cluster with 1GB of RAM, supporting advanced hybrid and vector search.

Cohere: Free developer keys for embeddings and Rerank APIs, very useful for enhancing RAG retrieval accuracy.

Hugging Face Spaces: Host your Python RAG demos (built with Streamlit, Gradio, or Chainlit) for free on standard CPU instances.

Developing mobile applications (e.g., using React Native or Flutter) requires builds and backend services.

Expo EAS (Expo Application Services): Free build tier to compile your React Native apps into Android (.apk/.aab) and iOS (.ipa) binaries without needing a powerful local machine or Mac.

Supabase: 2 free projects with a full PostgreSQL database, built-in Authentication, File Storage (up to 1GB), and Realtime capabilities.

Firebase (Spark Plan): Free hosting, Authentication, Cloud Firestore (NoSQL database), and Cloud Storage. Excellent integration with mobile frameworks.

Deploying web frontends and backends.

Vercel: The best platform for hosting React, Next.js, and static websites. Includes a free hobby tier with automatic CI/CD from GitHub.

Netlify: Free tier for static websites and serverless functions, featuring instant rollbacks and form handling.

Render: Free tier for hosting web services (Node.js, Python, Go, Rust), static sites, and PostgreSQL databases (note: free servers spin down after 15 minutes of inactivity).

GitHub Pages: Completely free hosting for static sites (pure HTML/JS or built sites like single page apps) directly from GitHub repos.

Ingesting, storing, and transforming data.

MotherDuck: Free serverless DuckDB in the cloud. Includes 10GB of storage and makes querying local or remote files fast using analytical SQL.

Google BigQuery Sandbox: No credit card required. Gives you 10GB of active storage and 1TB of query processing per month.

Mage.ai / Airbyte (Local): Open-source pipelines that you can run locally for free to orchestrate and ingest data.

Creating and sharing dashboards.

Streamlit Community Cloud: Connects to your GitHub repository and deploys your Streamlit Python dashboards for free.

Looker Studio: Free to use with native Google connectors (Google Sheets, BigQuery, Google Analytics) to design interactive dashboards.

Tableau Public: Free service to publish and share Tableau visualizations publicly.

Gradio: Free deployment of interactive machine learning interfaces directly on Hugging Face Spaces.

Practical tools to build, host and scaffold projects quickly.
